title: Shoes off, right foot in
hookLine: shoes at the door, enter with the right foot, a greeting prayer on the lips

lines: A PILE OF SHOES AT THE MOSQUE.
cards: A row of shoes by a front door says a lot about a house. A neat rack in a friend's hallway. A basket of slippers.
Grandma's mat, where nobody gets past in sneakers. Step out of your shoes and you step out of the outside world, literally, and your feet land on something softer.

At a mosque door the pile is bigger: a long shelf, or just a heap, of sneakers, loafers, tiny children's sandals, work boots. That pile is the first thing a visitor meets. Today: shoes off, right foot in.

teach.h: SHOES OFF: FACES GO ON THIS FLOOR.
teach.b: Why shoes off? The simplest answer is the floor. In a mosque, people put their foreheads on that carpet five times a day, and you wouldn't walk across a kitchen table in the shoes you wore through a parking lot.

It isn't that shoes are forbidden in prayer as such. Bukhari reports that the companion Anas was asked whether the Prophet ﷺ ever prayed in his sandals, and he said yes; scholars add that the sandals must be clean.
But on a shared carpet, shoes off is the custom. Then the right foot.
Aisha said, in Bukhari, that the Prophet liked to begin with the right in everything he could: putting on his sandals, combing his hair, washing for prayer.
So it's customary to step into the mosque right foot first, and out left foot first. A small thing that turns an ordinary doorway into a moment you notice. Then the words.
Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet teaching that on entering the mosque one says: Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik.

teach.h: OPEN FOR ME THE DOORS OF YOUR MERCY.
teach.b: O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy. And on leaving: O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty. Mercy inside, bounty outside.
For a visitor, a few more things help. Modest, loose clothes. Mosques may ask women to cover their hair, and some keep scarves at the door.

teach.h: DON'T CROSS IN FRONT OF SOMEONE PRAYING.
teach.b: And don't walk directly in front of someone who's praying; wait, or go around behind them. None of it is a test.
It's what you do at grandma's: you come in gently.

how: At the mosque, Muslims leave their shoes at the door, step in with the right foot first saying 'Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik', and leave with the left foot, asking Allah for His bounty.

o: a rule that prayer in shoes is never allowed
a rule that only Muslims may walk on the carpet
shoes left at the door to keep the prayer floor clean

games.q: what's inside the mosque door — tap the pairs.
p: open for me the doors of Your mercy

s: the Prophet ﷺ never prayed in his sandals
Anas said he did (Bukhari); shoes off is about the shared carpet.
the words on entering ask for the doors of mercy
it's fine to walk directly in front of someone praying
the custom is to wait or pass behind them.

games.q: you've just arrived at the mosque door for the first time, shoes on. what do you do first?
o: take your shoes off and step in right foot first
wait outside until someone invites you to leave
games.why: shoes stay at the door because foreheads go on that floor, and the custom is to step in with the right foot, as the Prophet ﷺ liked to begin with the right.

practice: Walk to the nearest doorway, slipping off your shoes if it's easy, and pause at the threshold for one breath. Step through right foot first, and let the left follow.
If you pray, you can say as you step, Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik; if not, just notice the change: the air, the floor, the sound.

wordCard.voice: Shoes off. The first step into a mosque: shoes at the door, the right foot first, and a request for the doors of mercy. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy, said on entering the mosque.

carryVoice: Your line: come in gently. Mercy on the way in, bounty on the way out. See you tomorrow.
